claims.statement: Internal QC and external or peer assessment are established laboratory quality practices, so the underlying operational problem is real.
Lot-change verification is necessary, but QC material can be noncommutable with patient samples and pooled QC should not be marketed as conclusive clinical validation.
The generic interlaboratory peer-QC layer is already served by incumbents with automated submission, alerts, peer statistics, and reagent-lot reporting.
Standards make QC-result exchange technically conceivable, but omit several semantics and do not establish enabled access, contractual rights, privacy handling, or connector cost.

A human-reviewed QC incident packet with no patient-result release or lot disposition may have lower regulatory exposure than diagnostic interpretation, but the final intended purpose still needs qualified IVDR analysis.
A QC-only pipeline can reduce privacy exposure, but pseudonymized or re-identifiable data remains within GDPR and accidental patient identifiers must be prevented.
No gathered evidence proves distributor demand, data permission, low-cost integration, price, retention, or a path to enough analyzers for the wealth case.

contrary_evidence: Bio-Rad, Randox, and Technopath already provide much of the proposed peer comparison and connectivity surface.
QC material can diverge from patient-sample behavior across reagent lots, constraining the meaning of alerts.
The IVDR and MDCG guidance make intended purpose and output interpretation material regulatory gates.
The connectivity standard does not cover calibration, nomenclature, or privacy and grants no interface permission.
